title: Oil level keeps dropping
h1: Why does my car keep losing oil?
metaDesc: Oil level keeps dropping or your car is burning oil? Answer a few questions to see if it's a leak, worn seals or rings, or something urgent, and what to do next.
intro: Oil that keeps going low is either leaking out or being burned inside the engine. Both can be slow and manageable at first, but running an engine low on oil can destroy it quickly. Answer the questions below to find where the oil is likely going, how urgent it is, and what to tell your mechanic.
safety: If the red oil pressure light comes on while driving, pull over safely and shut the engine off right away.
If you see smoke or flames from under the hood, pull over, turn off the engine, get everyone out and call 911.
If the engine starts knocking or ticking loudly, stop driving and check the oil before going any further.

q_level.q: Is the oil pressure light on, or how low is the oil on the dipstick?
q_level.help: The oil pressure light is red and usually looks like an old-fashioned oil can. Check the dipstick with the car on level ground, a few minutes after shutting off the engine. Some cars show the oil level on the dash instead of a dipstick.

opts.a: The oil pressure light is on or flickers, or there's little or no oil on the dipstick
It's low, or I keep having to add oil between changes
I haven't checked / I'm not sure

q_where.q: Do you see any signs of where the oil is going?

opts.a: Oil spots under the car, or oily, wet areas on the engine
A burning oil smell from under the hood, or light smoke from the engine area
Oily film in the coolant reservoir, or the coolant level is dropping too
No drips, no smoke, no smell: the oil just disappears

q_smoke_when.q: When do you see the blue-gray smoke?
q_smoke_when.help: Burning oil smoke is bluish-gray and has a sharp, acrid smell. Thin white vapor on a cold morning that disappears after a few minutes is normal condensation.

opts.a: A puff at startup, especially after the car sat overnight, then it clears
Steadily while driving, and more when accelerating
The engine has a turbo, and there's smoke under acceleration or a whistling or whining sound

result.title: The engine may be dangerously low on oil
result.now: If you're driving, pull over when it's safe. Shut the engine off and don't run it until you've added the correct oil to the full mark. If the oil pressure light stays on after that, have it towed.
if: If the engine was knocking or ticking loudly before you stopped, have it towed even after adding oil. There may already be damage.

If the oil pressure light came on while the engine was running, have the engine checked before driving it again, even if the light goes off after topping up. Low oil pressure can damage the engine before any noise shows up.

If the oil light never came on and the dipstick now reads full, topping up is the first step, but it isn't proof the engine is unharmed. Call a shop to find where the oil went, and check the level before every start until then.
If you see smoke from under the hood, or the temperature gauge is high, don't restart the engine.
result.why: Oil protects every moving part of the engine. When there's too little, oil pressure drops and metal parts start grinding against each other. Running the engine like this for even a short time can ruin it.

causes.name: Oil consumed or leaked over time without being topped up
causes.clues: It's been a long time since the last oil change or check.

causes.name: Sudden large leak
causes.clues: A fresh puddle under the car, or oil sprayed under the hood.

causes.name: Oil pump or pressure problem
causes.clues: The oil pressure light is on even though the dipstick shows full. A shop will usually test oil pressure with a gauge before replacing a sensor or pump.

you: With the engine off, check the dipstick on level ground.
Look under the car for a fresh puddle.
shop: Oil pressure test with a gauge
Check for engine damage, such as bearing noise

result.title: Check the oil level the right way first
result.now: Park on level ground, turn the engine off, wait a few minutes, then pull the dipstick, wipe it, push it fully back in and pull it out again to read the level.
if: If the oil is below the low mark, add the oil type listed in your owner's manual a little at a time until it reaches the full mark.
If you find yourself adding oil more than once between oil changes, have it checked to find out where it's going.
If the oil pressure light comes on at any point, stop driving and shut the engine off.
If the engine knocks or ticks loudly, don't drive it until it's checked.
result.why: Readings taken on a slope or right after shutdown can look lower than the real level. A correct reading tells you whether there's really a problem, and how fast the oil is going down.

causes.name: Normal oil use between changes
causes.clues: A small drop over thousands of miles, with no smoke or leaks.

causes.name: Slow leak
causes.clues: Spots under the car where it's usually parked.

causes.name: Engine burning oil
causes.clues: Blue-gray smoke from the tailpipe.

you: Check the oil level on level ground with the engine off.
Write down the mileage each time you add oil, and how much you added.

result.title: The engine may be leaking oil
result.now: Keep the oil topped up to the full mark, check it every time you fill up with fuel, and book a leak inspection when convenient.
if: If the drips are bigger than a coin each day or form a puddle, get it checked within a few days.
If you smell burning oil or see smoke from under the hood, don't keep driving. Oil on a hot exhaust can catch fire. Pull over, turn off the engine and have it checked before driving further.
If the oil level drops below the low mark between checks, stop driving and add oil before going further.
If the oil pressure light comes on, pull over and shut the engine off right away.
result.why: Oil spots under the car or wet, grimy areas on the engine usually mean oil is escaping from a gasket or seal. Small leaks are common on older engines, but they tend to get worse and can leave the engine low on oil. A shop will usually clean the area or use dye to find the exact source before replacing a gasket.

causes.name: Leaking valve cover gasket
causes.clues: Oil on the top or sides of the engine, sometimes with a burning smell.

causes.name: Leaking oil pan gasket or drain plug
causes.clues: Drips from the very bottom of the engine, or a leak that started after an oil change.

causes.name: Oil filter loose or its seal damaged
causes.clues: A leak that started right after an oil change.

causes.name: Leaking front or rear main seal
causes.clues: Oil at the front of the engine near the belts, or where the engine meets the transmission.

you: Put cardboard under the engine overnight and note where the drips land.
Check that the oil filler cap is on tight.
shop: Leak inspection, often with a UV dye
Engine cleaning and recheck to pinpoint the source

result.title: Oil may be leaking onto hot engine or exhaust parts
result.now: Don't drive it until the source is found. Let the engine cool fully, check the oil level, then have it towed or ask a mobile mechanic to look at it.
if: If you see more than light wisps of smoke, or any flames, pull over, shut the engine off and get everyone out.
If the smell is strong inside the cabin, open the windows and keep the engine off until it's checked.
If the smell started right after an oil change and you see no smoke, spilled oil burning off is possible. Call the shop that did the change and have them check it before you rely on the car.
If the oil pressure light comes on or the oil is below the low mark, don't start the engine.
result.why: A burning oil smell or light smoke from under the hood often means oil is dripping onto the hot exhaust manifold or engine. A valve cover gasket is a common source. Besides losing oil, it's a fire risk, and there's no way to tell from the driver's seat how much is reaching the exhaust.

causes.name: Leaking valve cover gasket
causes.clues: Oil seeping from the top edge of the engine, with smoke near the exhaust manifold.

causes.name: Oil spilled during an oil change
causes.clues: The smell started right after an oil change and fades within a few drives.
causes.against: If the smell keeps coming back, a real leak is more likely.

causes.name: Leaking oil filter housing or oil cooler seal
causes.clues: Oil collecting near the filter area, sometimes running down onto the exhaust.

you: With the engine cold, look for wet oil on top of the engine and around the exhaust manifold.
Check that the oil filler cap is tight.
shop: Oil filter housing and cooler seal check

result.title: Oil may be mixing with coolant, possibly from a head gasket or oil cooler
result.now: Stop driving it. Check the oil and coolant levels with the engine cold, and have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If the temperature gauge has been climbing, don't start the engine again until it's been checked.
If the oil on the dipstick looks milky or like light-brown chocolate milk, coolant is getting into the oil too.
If you see steam or white smoke from under the hood or the tailpipe, keep the engine off.
result.why: Oil and coolant run in separate passages and should never mix. An oily film in the coolant often points to a failed head gasket or oil cooler. Mixed fluids lose their ability to lubricate and cool, and driving on can cause overheating and serious engine damage. A shop will usually pressure test the cooling system before deciding what needs repair.

causes.name: Blown head gasket
causes.clues: Overheating, white exhaust smoke with a sweet smell, or bubbles in the coolant reservoir.

causes.name: Failed oil cooler
causes.clues: Oil in the coolant without overheating, on engines that have an oil cooler.

causes.name: Cracked cylinder head or engine block
causes.clues: Severe overheating in the past.
causes.against: Less common than a head gasket or oil cooler.

you: With the engine cold, look in the coolant reservoir for an oily or brown film.
Check the dipstick for milky oil.

result.title: The engine may be burning oil slowly inside
result.now: Keep the oil at the full mark, write down the mileage each time you add oil, and book a check when convenient.
if: If you're adding about a quart every 1,000 miles or more, that's at the high end of what most engines should use. Get it checked sooner.
If the check engine light comes on or the engine starts to misfire, oil may be fouling the spark plugs. Have it checked soon.
If your engine has a known oil-consumption problem, ask the dealer about recalls or service bulletins.
If the oil pressure light comes on or the engine starts knocking, pull over and shut it off right away.
result.why: Many engines use some oil between changes, and burning a small amount may produce no smoke you can see. Worn piston rings, worn valve seals or a clogged crankcase ventilation (PCV) valve can raise oil use gradually. Keeping a log tells the shop whether it's normal or getting worse.

causes.name: Clogged or stuck PCV valve
causes.clues: Oil residue in the air intake, oil leaks starting in several places, or a whistling noise.

causes.name: Worn or stuck piston rings
causes.clues: High mileage, fewer oil changes than recommended, or a known engine design issue.

causes.name: Worn valve stem seals
causes.clues: A puff of smoke at startup now and then.

causes.name: Slow leak you can't see yet
causes.clues: Oil drips that only show up on the highway and are blown away.

you: Log the mileage and amount each time you add oil.
Look at the tailpipe for black, oily soot.
Make sure you're using the oil type and viscosity in the owner's manual.
shop: Spark plug inspection for oil fouling

result.title: Worn valve stem seals are a likely cause
result.now: Keep the oil topped up, note how often you add it, and book a check when convenient.
if: If the smoke starts showing up while driving too, the piston rings may also be worn. Get it checked sooner.
If the engine misfires or the check engine light comes on, have it checked within a few days.
If the oil pressure light comes on, pull over and shut the engine off right away.
result.why: Valve stem seals keep oil from running down into the cylinders. When they harden with age, oil seeps in while the car sits, and burns off as a puff of blue smoke at startup. It usually develops slowly, but the oil level still needs watching, because running low on oil is what damages engines. A shop will usually do a consumption test before recommending seal work.

causes.name: Worn or hardened valve stem seals
causes.clues: A puff of blue smoke at startup after sitting, then clear.
causes.against: If the smoke continues while driving, rings are more likely.

causes.name: Worn valve guides
causes.clues: Higher mileage, or ticking from the top of the engine.

causes.name: Turbo seal seepage (turbo engines)
causes.clues: The engine has a turbocharger.

you: Watch the tailpipe during a cold start.
Log how much oil you add and when.

result.title: Worn piston rings or a ventilation problem are possible
result.now: Check the oil level every time you fill up with fuel, keep it at the full mark, and have the engine checked within the next few days.
if: If the smoke is heavy or the oil drops fast enough to need oil every few days, don't drive it until it's checked.
If the check engine light flashes or the engine shakes, stop driving it. Oil may be fouling the spark plugs and damaging the catalytic converter.
If the oil pressure light comes on or the engine starts knocking, pull over and shut it off right away.
result.why: Steady blue smoke while driving usually means oil is getting into the cylinders and burning. Worn piston rings are one cause. A clogged ventilation (PCV) valve can push oil into the intake and cause the same symptom, and it's a much simpler fix, so a shop will usually check it before any engine work.

causes.name: Clogged PCV valve or crankcase ventilation problem
causes.clues: Oil in the air intake tube, or oil leaks appearing in several places.

causes.name: Worn or stuck piston rings
causes.clues: High mileage, low power, or smoke that gets worse under load.

causes.name: Worn valve guides or seals
causes.clues: Smoke is also worse at startup or when slowing down.

you: Watch the tailpipe while someone accelerates firmly.
Log the mileage and amount each time you add oil.

result.title: The turbocharger seals may be leaking oil
result.now: Check and top up the oil, then have the turbo checked within the next few days. Drive gently and avoid hard acceleration until then.
if: If the smoke is heavy, the whining turns into a grinding or siren-like noise, or power drops suddenly, stop driving and have it towed.
If the engine revs up on its own and won't shut off, get away from the vehicle and call for help.
If the oil pressure light comes on, pull over and shut the engine off right away.
result.why: A turbo spins very fast on a thin film of engine oil. When its seals or bearings wear, oil can be pushed into the intake or exhaust and burned, which shows up as blue smoke under boost. A failing turbo can come apart and damage the engine. A shop will usually check the oil return line and ventilation system before replacing the turbo.

causes.name: Worn turbocharger seals or bearings
causes.clues: Blue smoke under acceleration, a whistle or whine, and oil in the intake piping.

causes.name: Restricted turbo oil return line
causes.clues: Oil leaking from the turbo area.

causes.name: Clogged crankcase ventilation (PCV) system
causes.clues: Oil in the intake piping even though the turbo has no play.

you: Note whether the smoke is worst under acceleration.
Listen for a new whine or whistle from the engine.

result.title: Keep the oil topped up and have the source tracked down
result.now: Top up the oil to the full mark, check it every time you fill up with fuel, and book an inspection when convenient.
if: If the oil drops below the low mark between checks, get it checked within a few days.
If the oil pressure light comes on, pull over and shut the engine off right away.
If you see smoke from under the hood or the engine starts knocking, pull over and shut it off.
result.why: Oil only goes two places: out through a leak or into the engine where it burns. A shop can quickly look for leaks and test whether the engine is burning oil. Your record of how often you add oil helps them a lot.

causes.name: Slow oil leak
causes.clues: Spots where the car is parked, or oily areas on the engine.

causes.name: Engine burning oil
causes.clues: Blue-gray exhaust smoke, or oily soot in the tailpipe.

causes.name: Clogged PCV valve
causes.clues: Oil use that crept up over time.

you: Log how much oil you add and at what mileage.
Put cardboard under the engine overnight.
